intro: Practice the points free-response graders most often see missed: naming the variables, choosing the control that isolates the variable and saying what it rules out, writing null and alternative hypotheses, telling claim from evidence from reasoning, and predicting a result with the mechanism behind it. Each scenario gives real-looking data. The choice drills are checked part by part; the written answers are scored by you against a rubric, with a model answer.
howItWorks:
• Independent variable: what the investigator changes on purpose. Dependent variable: what is measured in response. Controlled variables: everything kept the same. A confounding variable differs between groups by accident and could explain the result.
  • A control is the group or step that removes one other explanation. Several controls can be sensible; the best one matches the test groups in everything except the factor you need to rule out. Saying what a control rules out earns its own point.
  • Null hypothesis: the independent variable has no effect, so there is no difference in the dependent variable among the groups. Alternative hypothesis: there is an effect (with or without a direction). Data support or fail to support a hypothesis; they never prove it.
  • Claim answers the question. Evidence is data: values, comparisons, error bars, a test statistic. Reasoning is the biology that explains why the evidence supports the claim.
  • Prediction says what will happen; the mechanism says why, in biological terms. Each is scored separately.
  • Write it yourself: write your answer first, then open the rubric, tick each point you earned and compare with the model answer.

drills.name: Controls and what they rule out

scenarios.title: Nitrogen supply and protein in duckweed
scenarios.setup: Duckweed is a tiny floating plant that takes up its nitrogen from the water as nitrate. A research team grows duckweed for 14 days in flasks of nutrient medium containing 0, 1, 2, 4 or 8 mM nitrate, supplied as potassium nitrate (KNO₃). Every flask gets the same light, temperature and volume of medium. Four flasks are grown at each nitrate level. At the end, the team dries the plants and measures the protein content of the dry mass.

data.caption: Duckweed after 14 days (mean ± SE, n = 4 flasks)

options: Concentration of nitrate in the medium
Protein content of the dried plants
Light and temperature in the growth chamber
Number of days the plants grow
Volume of medium in each flask

why.iv: The team set five nitrate levels on purpose: nitrate is what they changed.
why.dv: Protein content is measured at the end to see the effect of nitrate.

control.q: Potassium nitrate adds potassium as well as nitrate, so the 8 mM flasks also get 8 mM more potassium than the 0 mM flasks. Which change to the design best isolates the effect of nitrogen?
options: Add potassium chloride so every flask has the same total potassium
Add flasks of each medium with no plants, to measure any nitrate lost without uptake
Grow extra flasks with no nitrate and no potassium at all
Supply the nitrate as calcium nitrate instead of potassium nitrate
why: Right: with potassium equal in every flask, only the nitrate differs, so a change in protein can be credited to nitrogen.
Flasks without plants check whether nitrate disappears from the medium on its own; they do nothing about the extra potassium that rises with nitrate.
This group lacks two nutrients at once, so any difference could come from either one; it cannot separate potassium from nitrogen.
This swaps one confound for another: calcium would now rise with nitrate, just as potassium did.

controlWhy.q: What does giving every flask the same potassium rule out?
options: That the extra potassium, not the extra nitrogen, caused the rise in protein
That the plants in different flasks received different amounts of light and warmth
That duckweed makes some protein even when no nitrate is added
That the protein assay gives inaccurate readings at low protein levels
why: Right: potassium also supports plant growth, so without this change the extra potassium could explain part of the rise.
Light was already the same for every flask; equalizing potassium has nothing to do with it.
The 0 mM group already shows the protein level without added nitrate; equalizing potassium does not change that.
Assay accuracy is checked with samples of known protein content, not by changing what the plants are given.

slots.label: How the statement starts
options: There is no difference
There is a difference
There is a steady increase
why: Right: a null hypothesis says the independent variable has no effect, so it predicts no difference.
That is the alternative hypothesis, the effect the experiment looks for. The null says there is none.
A null hypothesis predicts no effect at all, not an effect in one direction.

slots.label: What is (not) different
options: in protein content per gram of dry mass
in the nitrate concentration of the media
in the light and temperature the flasks receive
why: Right: this is the dependent variable, the thing the null hypothesis says will not differ.
This is the independent variable. The investigators made it differ on purpose; the hypothesis is about its effect on what is measured.
This was kept the same on purpose (a controlled variable), so it is not what the hypothesis is about.

slots.label: Among which groups
options: among duckweed grown at different nitrate concentrations
between flasks with and without potassium
between day 1 and day 14 of growth
why: Right: the groups differ only in nitrate, the independent variable.
Potassium is not the independent variable; once it is equalized every flask has the same amount.
Time is the same for every group; the hypothesis compares the nitrate groups, not days.

alt.q: Which is a suitable alternative hypothesis for this experiment?
options: Duckweed grown with more nitrate has more protein per gram of dry mass
Nitrate concentration has no effect on the protein content of duckweed
The experiment will prove that plants need nitrogen to make protein
Duckweed grown with more nitrate stores more potassium in its tissues
why: Right: it states an effect of the independent variable on the dependent variable, with a direction, and it can be tested.
That is the null hypothesis: it states no effect.
Data can support a hypothesis or fail to support it; no experiment proves one.
Potassium in the plants was not measured; this experiment's hypothesis is about protein.

cer.text: Raising nitrate increases the protein content of duckweed up to about 4 mM, with little further gain at 8 mM.
cer.why: This is the claim: it answers how nitrate affects protein.

cer.text: Mean protein rose from 92 mg/g at 0 mM to 241 mg/g at 4 mM.
cer.why: This is evidence: it reports values from the table.

cer.text: The 4 mM and 8 mM means (241 and 248 mg/g) differ by less than the standard error of either group.
cer.why: This is evidence: it compares the data with their spread. Comparing means with SEs is still describing data, not explaining it.

cer.text: Every amino acid has a nitrogen-containing amino group, so plants short of nitrogen cannot build as many amino acids or proteins.
cer.why: This is reasoning: it gives the biology that links nitrate to protein.

cer.text: Once nitrogen is no longer scarce, another resource limits growth, so extra nitrate adds little protein.
cer.why: This is reasoning: it explains, with biology, why the curve levels off.

predict.q: The team grows new flasks at 4 mM nitrate in a medium with no sulfate, the plants' only sulfur source, with potassium equalized and everything else unchanged. Predict the protein content compared with the original 4 mM flasks.
options: Lower
Higher
About the same
why: Right: two amino acids, cysteine and methionine, contain sulfur, and almost every protein contains them, so the plants cannot complete most proteins.
Removing a building block of some amino acids cannot raise the amount of protein made.
Nitrogen is not the only element proteins need: without sulfur, the sulfur-containing amino acids cannot be made.

options: Without sulfur the plants cannot make cysteine or methionine, so proteins that contain them cannot be finished
Without sulfate the plants hold more water, so their protein is diluted
Sulfur atoms form the peptide bonds that join amino acids together
Without sulfate the plants use their nitrogen for nucleic acids instead of protein
why: Right: sulfur is part of the R groups of these two amino acids.
Protein is measured per gram of dry mass, so water content cannot dilute it.
A peptide bond joins the carboxyl carbon of one amino acid to the amino nitrogen of the next; sulfur sits in some R groups, not in the backbone.
There is no such trade; the missing sulfur blocks the sulfur-containing amino acids themselves.

write.prompt: Using the data in the table, make a claim that answers the question the investigators asked, support it with evidence (specific values with units), and give the reasoning that explains why the evidence supports the claim. The question: how does nitrate supply affect the protein content of duckweed?

rubric.point: Claim: protein content rises with nitrate supply, leveling off above about 4 mM.
accept: More nitrate gives more protein per gram
Nitrogen limits protein content at low nitrate

rubric.point: Evidence: cites values from the table, such as 92 mg/g at 0 mM rising to 241 mg/g at 4 mM, or the small 4 mM to 8 mM difference compared with the SEs.
accept: Any correct comparison of two means with units

rubric.point: Reasoning: amino acids contain nitrogen (in the amino group), so the nitrogen supply limits how much protein the plants can build.
accept: Nitrogen is needed to make amino acids
Proteins are made of nitrogen-containing monomers

write.sample: Protein content increases with nitrate supply up to about 4 mM and then levels off. Mean protein rose from 92 mg/g dry mass at 0 mM to 241 mg/g at 4 mM, but was 248 mg/g at 8 mM, a difference smaller than either group's SE. Each amino acid has a nitrogen-containing amino group, so when nitrate is scarce the plants cannot make as many amino acids or proteins; above 4 mM something else limits growth.

write.prompt: The team moves plants from the 8 mM flasks into medium with no nitrate for 7 days, keeping everything else the same. The plants keep photosynthesizing and adding carbohydrate. Predict how protein per gram of dry mass changes, and explain your prediction.

rubric.point: Prediction: protein per gram of dry mass decreases.
accept: Protein content falls
Lower protein percentage

rubric.point: Mechanism: with no new nitrogen the plants cannot make new amino acids, so little new protein is made while carbohydrate keeps adding dry mass.
accept: No nitrogen means no new amino acids, so protein is spread over more mass

write.sample: Protein per gram of dry mass will fall. Without nitrate the plants have no new nitrogen to build amino acids, so they make little new protein, but photosynthesis keeps adding carbohydrate, so the same protein is spread over more dry mass.

scenarios.title: Double bonds and melting point
scenarios.setup: A lab measures the melting point of four pure fats (triglycerides) with a calorimeter that heats each 5 mg sample at 2 °C per minute. In every fat, all three fatty acid tails are 18 carbons long; the fats differ only in how many cis double bonds each tail has. Each fat is measured three times.

data.caption: Melting points of 18-carbon fats (mean ± SE, n = 3)

options: Number of double bonds in each fatty acid tail
Melting point of the fat
Number of carbons in each fatty acid tail
Rate at which the calorimeter heats the sample
Mass of each sample

why.iv: The lab chose fats with 0, 1, 2 and 3 double bonds per tail: that is what differs on purpose.
why.dv: Melting point is what the calorimeter measures for each fat.

control.q: A student suggests a quicker study using butter, olive oil, sunflower oil and linseed oil. Which set of fats best isolates the effect of double bonds on melting point?
options: Fats whose tails are all 18 carbons long, with 0, 1, 2 or 3 double bonds per tail
Butter, olive oil, sunflower oil and linseed oil, which run from saturated to highly unsaturated
Saturated fats with tails 12, 14, 16 and 18 carbons long
One 18-carbon fat melted at several different heating rates
why: Right: with tail length fixed, the only difference among the fats is the number of double bonds.
These natural fats are mixtures that differ in tail length and in their blend of fatty acids, so a difference could come from either.
This set tests tail length, a different independent variable; none of these fats has a double bond.
This tests the method, not the effect of double bonds.

controlWhy.q: What does using only 18-carbon tails rule out?
options: That differences in tail length, not double bonds, caused the differences in melting point
That the samples were heated at different rates
That some of the fat samples were contaminated with water, which would change their melting points
That fats with double bonds melt at lower temperatures
why: Right: longer tails also raise melting point, so tail length had to be held constant.
Heating rate was already set the same by the calorimeter; tail length is a separate matter.
Contamination is prevented by handling, not by choosing tail length.
That is the effect being tested; a control helps show it, it does not rule it out.

slots.label: How the statement starts
options: There is no difference
There is a difference
There is a decrease
why: Right: a null hypothesis says the independent variable has no effect, so it predicts no difference.
That is the alternative hypothesis, the effect the experiment looks for. The null says there is none.
A null hypothesis predicts no effect at all, not an effect in one direction.

slots.label: What is (not) different
options: in melting point
in the number of double bonds per tail
in the length of the fatty acid tails
why: Right: this is the dependent variable, the thing the null hypothesis says will not differ.
This is the independent variable. The investigators made it differ on purpose; the hypothesis is about its effect on what is measured.
This was kept the same on purpose (a controlled variable), so it is not what the hypothesis is about.

slots.label: Among which groups
options: among fats whose tails have different numbers of double bonds
between fats and oils at room temperature
among samples heated at different rates
why: Right: the fats differ only in double bonds, the independent variable.
Room temperature state is not what was measured; the groups are set by the number of double bonds.
Heating rate was the same for every sample, so it does not define the groups.

alt.q: Which is a suitable alternative hypothesis for this experiment?
options: Fats with more double bonds per tail have lower melting points
The number of double bonds has no effect on melting point
Fats with longer tails have higher melting points
A fat's melting point determines how many double bonds its tails have
why: Right: it states a testable effect of the independent variable on the dependent variable.
That is the null hypothesis: it states no effect.
Tail length was held constant here, so this experiment cannot test it.
This reverses cause and effect: the structure is fixed, and melting point is measured in response.

cer.text: Each added cis double bond lowers the melting point of an 18-carbon fat.
cer.why: This is the claim: it answers the question about double bonds and melting point.

cer.text: Melting point fell from 72.1 °C with no double bonds to 5.2 °C with one per tail.
cer.why: This is evidence: it reports values from the table.

cer.text: With two and three double bonds per tail it fell further, to −12.8 °C and −23.9 °C, and every SE is under 1 °C.
cer.why: This is evidence: more data, with their spread.

cer.text: A cis double bond puts a bend in the tail, so bent tails cannot pack closely together.
cer.why: This is reasoning: it explains with molecular structure.

cer.text: Loosely packed molecules have fewer attractions between them, so less heat is needed to separate them into a liquid.
cer.why: This is reasoning: it links packing to the melting point.

predict.q: Trielaidin also has three 18-carbon tails with one double bond each, but its double bonds are trans, which leaves each tail almost straight. Predict its melting point compared with triolein.
options: Higher
Lower
About the same
why: Right: nearly straight trans tails pack closely, much like saturated tails, so trielaidin melts well above triolein and is solid at room temperature.
A lower melting point would need tails that pack less tightly than bent cis tails; trans tails are straighter, not more bent.
The number of double bonds is the same, but the shape of the tail is not, and shape controls how closely tails pack.

options: Straight tails pack closely, so more attractions between molecules must be overcome to melt the fat
A trans double bond is a stronger covalent bond, so more heat is needed to break it as the fat melts
Trans tails carry more hydrogen atoms, so they form more hydrogen bonds with each other
Trans tails are more polar, so neighboring molecules attract each other more strongly
why: Right: melting separates whole molecules; tighter packing means more attractions to overcome.
Melting does not break covalent bonds inside a molecule; it separates molecules from one another.
Both fats have the same atoms; fatty acid tails are nonpolar and do not hydrogen bond with each other.
Cis and trans tails are both nonpolar hydrocarbon chains; the difference is shape, not polarity.

write.prompt: Using the data in the table, make a claim that answers the question the investigators asked, support it with evidence (specific values with units), and give the reasoning that explains why the evidence supports the claim. The question: how does the number of double bonds in fatty acid tails affect melting point?

rubric.point: Claim: more (cis) double bonds per tail give a lower melting point.
accept: Unsaturated fats melt at lower temperatures than saturated fats

rubric.point: Evidence: cites values, such as 72.1 °C with no double bonds versus 5.2 °C with one, or the fall to −23.9 °C with three.
accept: Any correct pair of values with units

rubric.point: Reasoning: cis double bonds bend the tails so they cannot pack closely, leaving fewer attractions between molecules to overcome.
accept: Kinks prevent close packing
Weaker attractions between bent tails

write.sample: More cis double bonds per tail lower a fat's melting point. Tristearin, with no double bonds, melted at 72.1 °C, triolein with one per tail at 5.2 °C and trilinolenin with three at −23.9 °C. Each cis double bond bends the tail, so the molecules cannot pack closely and have fewer attractions between them, and less heat is needed to melt the fat.

write.prompt: A food company adds hydrogen to triolein until no double bonds are left. Predict the melting point of the product compared with triolein, and explain your prediction.

rubric.point: Prediction: the melting point rises (to about that of tristearin, 72 °C).
accept: Higher melting point
It becomes solid at room temperature

rubric.point: Mechanism: with the double bonds gone the tails are straight and pack closely, so more attractions between molecules must be overcome to melt it.
accept: Saturated tails pack tightly

write.sample: The melting point will rise to about 72 °C, because removing every double bond turns triolein into tristearin. Without the bends, the straight saturated tails pack closely, so there are more attractions between molecules to overcome before the fat melts.

scenarios.title: Salt and the contractile vacuole
scenarios.setup: Paramecium is a single-celled freshwater organism. Water keeps entering it by osmosis, and an organelle called the contractile vacuole collects water and squeezes it out of the cell. A student places paramecia in pond water with 0, 25, 50, 75 or 100 mM added sodium chloride (NaCl), waits 15 minutes, then counts how many times the contractile vacuole of one cell empties in 1 minute. Ten cells are timed at each concentration, all at 22 °C.

data.caption: Contractile vacuole emptying rate (mean ± SE, n = 10 cells)

options: Concentration of NaCl added to the pond water
Number of times the contractile vacuole empties per minute
Time the cells spend in each solution before timing
Temperature of the slides
Number of cells timed at each concentration

why.iv: The student chose the five NaCl concentrations: that is what changes on purpose.
why.dv: The emptying rate is what the student counts in response.

whyOptions: That is the sample size. Timing ten cells per group makes each mean more reliable; it is not a factor that could cause the effect.

control.q: Sodium and chloride ions might slow the vacuole by harming the cell, not by changing water movement. Which added group would best test this?
options: Paramecia in sucrose solutions with the same total solute concentration as each NaCl solution
Paramecia in pond water with no added NaCl
Paramecia in 100 mM NaCl timed after 60 minutes instead of 15
Paramecia in distilled water, which has even fewer dissolved solutes than the pond water they came from
why: Right: sucrose changes the solute concentration without adding sodium or chloride. If the vacuole slows by the same amount, the effect comes from water movement, not the ions.
This group is already in the experiment (0 mM). It shows the baseline but cannot separate an ion effect from a solute effect.
A longer wait tests how the response changes with time; the cells still face the same ions, so both explanations remain.
This extends the range the other way; it gives no way to tell harm from the ions apart from osmosis.

controlWhy.q: If the sucrose groups slow just as much as the matching NaCl groups, what does that rule out?
options: That a toxic effect of sodium or chloride ions slowed the vacuole
That the contractile vacuole pumps water out of the cell
That water enters paramecia by osmosis in pond water
That the student miscounted emptyings at high NaCl concentrations
why: Right: sucrose has no sodium or chloride, so a matching slow-down points to the solute concentration, through osmosis.
That is how the vacuole works; the control does not test or rule it out.
The sucrose result supports this idea; it does not rule it out.
Counting errors are reduced by careful technique and repeats, not by a different solute.

slots.label: How the statement starts
options: There is no difference
There is a difference
There is a decrease
why: Right: a null hypothesis says the independent variable has no effect, so it predicts no difference.
That is the alternative hypothesis, the effect the experiment looks for. The null says there is none.
A null hypothesis predicts no effect at all, not an effect in one direction.

slots.label: What is (not) different
options: in how often the contractile vacuole empties
in the NaCl concentration of the solutions
in the temperature of the slides
why: Right: this is the dependent variable, the thing the null hypothesis says will not differ.
This is the independent variable. The investigators made it differ on purpose; the hypothesis is about its effect on what is measured.
This was kept the same on purpose (a controlled variable), so it is not what the hypothesis is about.

slots.label: Among which groups
options: among paramecia in different NaCl concentrations
between NaCl solutions and sucrose solutions
before and after each cell is placed on the slide
why: Right: the groups differ only in NaCl, the independent variable.
Sucrose is the proposed control, not the independent variable of the original experiment.
This compares times, not the groups the independent variable sets up.

alt.q: Which is a suitable alternative hypothesis for this experiment?
options: Paramecia in higher NaCl concentrations empty their contractile vacuoles less often
NaCl concentration has no effect on how often the contractile vacuole empties
Paramecia in higher NaCl concentrations will take in water until they swell and burst
The vacuole empties less often because the cell wants to keep its water
why: Right: a testable effect of the independent variable on the dependent variable.
That is the null hypothesis.
Water leaves cells in a more concentrated solution; and the hypothesis should be about the vacuole rate that was measured.
Cells do not want things; this states a purpose, not a testable relationship between the variables.

cer.text: The more concentrated the outside solution, the less often the contractile vacuole empties.
cer.why: This is the claim.

cer.text: The mean rate fell from 8.4 emptyings per minute in pond water to 1.1 per minute in 100 mM NaCl.
cer.why: This is evidence: values from the table.

cer.text: Each 25 mM step lowered the rate, and the SEs (0.2 to 0.4) are small compared with the gaps between groups.
cer.why: This is evidence: it describes the pattern and spread of the data.

cer.text: A more concentrated outside solution has a lower water potential, so less water enters the cell by osmosis.
cer.why: This is reasoning: it applies water potential.

cer.text: With less water entering, the vacuole takes longer to fill, so it empties less often.
cer.why: This is reasoning: it links water entry to the measured rate.

predict.q: The student adds a chemical that stops the cell making ATP to paramecia in pond water with no added NaCl. The contractile vacuole needs ATP to work. Predict what happens to the cell's volume over the next 10 minutes.
options: Increases
Decreases
Stays about the same
why: Right: water keeps entering by osmosis, but nothing removes it, so the cell swells and may burst.
In pond water, water enters the cell, because the cytoplasm has a lower water potential than the pond water.
Osmosis needs no ATP, so water keeps entering after the vacuole stops.

options: Osmosis needs no ATP, so water still enters, but the stopped vacuole no longer removes it
Without ATP, aquaporins pump water into the cell faster
Without ATP, the cell wall can no longer resist the cell's expansion
Without ATP, the cell makes extra solutes that lower its water potential and pull more water inside
why: Right: passive water entry continues while the energy-using removal stops.
Aquaporins are channels: water moves through them passively, and they use no ATP.
Paramecium has no cell wall, which is why it needs a contractile vacuole.
Making molecules takes energy; a cell short of ATP does not build up extra solutes.

write.prompt: Using the data in the table, make a claim that answers the question the investigators asked, support it with evidence (specific values with units), and give the reasoning that explains why the evidence supports the claim. The question: how does the solute concentration outside the cell affect the contractile vacuole?

rubric.point: Claim: higher NaCl concentration outside lowers the emptying rate.
accept: The vacuole empties less often in saltier water

rubric.point: Evidence: cites values, such as 8.4 per minute at 0 mM falling to 1.1 per minute at 100 mM.
accept: Any correct comparison of two means with units

rubric.point: Reasoning: a more concentrated solution has a lower water potential, so less water enters by osmosis and the vacuole fills more slowly.
accept: Smaller water potential difference means less osmosis into the cell

write.sample: A more concentrated outside solution makes the contractile vacuole empty less often. The rate fell from 8.4 emptyings per minute in pond water to 1.1 per minute in 100 mM NaCl. Added solute lowers the water potential outside, so less water moves into the cell by osmosis; the vacuole fills more slowly and needs to empty less often.

write.prompt: The student moves paramecia from 100 mM NaCl back into pond water. Predict the emptying rate in the first minutes after the move, and explain your prediction.

rubric.point: Prediction: the emptying rate increases (back toward or above 8 per minute).
accept: Faster emptying

rubric.point: Mechanism: pond water has a higher water potential than the cytoplasm, so water enters faster by osmosis and the vacuole fills sooner.
accept: More water enters, so the vacuole must remove more

write.sample: The rate will rise. Pond water has a much higher water potential than the cell's cytoplasm, so water rushes in by osmosis and the vacuole fills, and empties, more often.

scenarios.title: Blocking the sodium-potassium pump
scenarios.setup: Red blood cells keep potassium ions (K⁺) high and sodium ions (Na⁺) low inside, using the sodium-potassium pump, which runs on ATP. A team suspends washed red blood cells in a buffered salt solution containing K⁺ and adds digoxin, a heart drug, at 0, 0.01, 0.1 or 1 µM. Digoxin barely dissolves in water, so the team dissolves it in ethanol and adds 10 µL of that stock to each digoxin tube; the 0 µM tubes get nothing. They measure K⁺ uptake by the cells over 1 hour at 37 °C, with five tubes per concentration.

data.caption: K⁺ uptake by red blood cells (mean ± SE, n = 5 tubes)
cols: K⁺ uptake (mmol per L of cells per hour)

options: Concentration of digoxin
Rate of K⁺ uptake by the cells
Temperature of the tubes
K⁺ concentration of the outside solution
Volume of ethanol added to the tube

why.iv: The team chose the four digoxin concentrations on purpose.
why.dv: K⁺ uptake is what they measure in response.

whyOptions: Not kept the same: only the digoxin tubes get ethanol. It differs between groups, so it is a possible confounding variable, not the independent variable.

control.q: The 0 µM tubes get no ethanol. Which added group best isolates the effect of digoxin?
options: Tubes given 10 µL of ethanol with no digoxin
Tubes kept at 4 °C, where the pump works very slowly
Tubes given 10 µM digoxin, to be sure the pump is fully blocked
Tubes of salt solution and digoxin with no red blood cells
why: Right: this solvent-only (vehicle) control gets everything the digoxin tubes get except the digoxin.
Cooling slows every process in the cell; it shows uptake with a slow pump but not whether ethanol changed the result.
A higher dose extends the dose range; every digoxin tube would still differ from the 0 µM tubes in ethanol as well.
Cell-free tubes check whether K⁺ disappears without cells; they say nothing about ethanol's effect on the cells.

controlWhy.q: What does the ethanol-only group rule out?
options: That the ethanol, not the digoxin, slowed K⁺ uptake
That some K⁺ enters the cells through other membrane proteins
That digoxin slows K⁺ uptake by binding to the pump
That the cells ran short of ATP during the hour
why: Right: if ethanol-only cells take up K⁺ like the 0 µM cells, the slow-down can be credited to digoxin.
Other routes are open in every tube; this control is about the solvent.
That is the explanation being tested; the control helps support it rather than ruling it out.
Every tube holds the same kind of cells using ATP the same way; the solvent control does not test ATP supply.

slots.label: How the statement starts
options: There is no difference
There is a difference
There is a decrease
why: Right: a null hypothesis says the independent variable has no effect, so it predicts no difference.
That is the alternative hypothesis, the effect the experiment looks for. The null says there is none.
A null hypothesis predicts no effect at all, not an effect in one direction.

slots.label: What is (not) different
options: in the rate of K⁺ uptake
in the digoxin concentration
in the temperature of the tubes
why: Right: this is the dependent variable, the thing the null hypothesis says will not differ.
This is the independent variable. The investigators made it differ on purpose; the hypothesis is about its effect on what is measured.
This was kept the same on purpose (a controlled variable), so it is not what the hypothesis is about.

slots.label: Among which groups
options: among cells given different concentrations of digoxin
between K⁺ and Na⁺ inside the cells
between red blood cells and plasma
why: Right: the groups differ in digoxin, the independent variable.
These are two ions, not the groups set up by the independent variable.
Plasma is not part of this experiment; the groups are the digoxin concentrations.

alt.q: Which is a suitable alternative hypothesis for this experiment?
options: Higher digoxin concentrations lower the rate of K⁺ uptake by red blood cells
Digoxin has no effect on the rate of K⁺ uptake
Red blood cells take up K⁺ because they need potassium to survive
The data will prove that digoxin slows K⁺ uptake by blocking the sodium-potassium pump
why: Right: a testable, directional effect of the independent variable on the dependent variable.
That is the null hypothesis.
This states a purpose, not a relationship between digoxin and uptake that the data can test.
No data prove a hypothesis; they support it or fail to.

cer.text: Digoxin slows K⁺ uptake by red blood cells, more so at higher concentrations.
cer.why: This is the claim.

cer.text: Uptake fell from 1.95 mmol per L of cells per hour with no digoxin to 0.28 at 1 µM.
cer.why: This is evidence: values from the table.

cer.text: Even 0.01 µM lowered uptake to 1.62, a gap several times the SEs of 0.06 and 0.07.
cer.why: This is evidence: a comparison using the data's spread.

cer.text: The sodium-potassium pump uses ATP to carry K⁺ into the cell against its concentration gradient, so blocking the pump cuts this active uptake.
cer.why: This is reasoning: it gives the transport mechanism.

predict.q: The team uses cells whose ATP has been used up, with no digoxin and no ethanol. Predict their K⁺ uptake compared with normal cells with no digoxin.
options: Lower
Higher
About the same
why: Right: without ATP the pump cannot carry K⁺ in against its gradient.

scenarios.title: Selection for surviving dry air
scenarios.setup: Starting from one large, genetically varied population of fruit flies, a team sets up eight lines. Four "dry" lines spend 6 hours in very dry air each generation, and only survivors breed. Four "humid" lines are handled the same way in humid air. After 30 generations the team raises every line for two generations in the same humid conditions, then measures how long females of the second generation survive in dry air with no food or water.

data.caption: Survival in dry air after 30 generations (mean ± SE, 50 females per line)

options: Humidity the lines are kept in each generation
Hours females survive in dry air
Number of generations of selection
Conditions in the final two generations before testing
Food given to every line

why.iv: The team assigned dry or humid treatment to each line on purpose.
why.dv: Survival time in dry air is what they measure at the end.

control.q: Flies that grew up in dry air, or whose mothers did, might survive longer without any change in their alleles. Which part of the design rules this out?
options: Raising every line for two generations in the same humid conditions before testing
Keeping four humid lines for the same 30 generations
Starting all eight lines from the same population
Testing only females
why: Right: the tested flies and their mothers all grew up in the same conditions, so a difference that remains reflects inherited (genetic) change.
The humid lines show what happens without dry selection, but on their own they cannot separate inherited change from effects of how the tested flies grew up.
This makes the lines start alike; it does not remove effects of the conditions the tested flies grew up in.
This removes differences between the sexes; it does not separate inherited change from growing conditions.

controlWhy.q: What do the two shared humid generations rule out?
options: That the dry lines survive longer only because of the conditions they or their mothers lived in
That the lines started with different allele frequencies
That chance changes in one line produced the difference
That very dry air kills fruit flies
why: Right: such effects fade after two generations in shared conditions, while changed allele frequencies remain.
Starting from one population handles that, not the final shared generations.
Having four lines of each kind handles chance; one line could drift, but all four would not drift the same way.
Dry air does kill flies; that is why survival is measured.

options: After 30 generations, flies from dry lines survive longer in dry air than flies from humid lines

Shorter
About the same

scenarios.title: Population size and allele frequency
scenarios.setup: A team studies a gene in flour beetles with two alleles, B (black body) and b (brown body). They start 20 populations of 10 beetles and 20 populations of 100 beetles, each with a B frequency of 0.50, all kept in identical jars. Each generation they choose 10 or 100 offspring at random to breed the next generation. After 20 generations they measure the frequency of B in every population.

data.caption: Frequency of B after 20 generations (20 populations of each size)

options: Number of beetles in each population
Spread of B frequency among populations after 20 generations
Starting frequency of B
Number of generations
Jars and food used

why.iv: The team set two population sizes on purpose.
why.dv: How far B frequencies spread, and how often an allele was lost, is what they measure.

control.q: If body color affects survival, selection rather than chance could change the allele frequencies. Which added group best tests whether the color alleles affect survival?
options: Populations of 1,000 beetles started at 0.50, in which chance changes are small
Another 20 populations of 10 beetles started at 0.50
Populations of 10 beetles started at a B frequency of 0.90 instead of 0.50
Populations of 10 black beetles only
why: Right: in very large populations drift is weak, so a steady shift in B would point to selection; no shift means the alleles act as neutral.
More small populations repeat the experiment; they cannot separate selection from drift any better.
This changes the starting frequency, a second variable, while drift stays strong.
With only one allele present there is no frequency change to measure.

That small populations lose alleles more often than large ones
That the beetles were chosen as breeders at random
That B is dominant to b
why: Right: without selection, the big shifts in small populations must come from random sampling.
That is the result being explained; the control does not rule it out.
Random choice is part of the method, not something the control tests.
Dominance is shown by crosses, not by allele frequencies over time.

between black and brown beetles

Population size has no effect on how much allele frequencies vary
Small populations evolve faster because they need to adapt more quickly
Small populations produce more mutations, so their allele frequencies change more

cer.text: Chance changed allele frequencies far more in small populations than in large ones.
